content.title: About
content.content: Chili with macaroni is a hearty dish that combines a spicy meat chili sauce with tender pasta. It is popular in the US and Russia as a quick, satisfying meal for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the mid‑20th century in American cafeterias where macaroni was used as an inexpensive side.
Spiciness can be adjusted by varying the amount of chili peppers, paprika, and spices, making it suitable for any palate.
Variations include adding beans, corn, cheese, or sour cream.
Chili with macaroni is often served in a single‑pot “casserole” style for camping or quick home cooking.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat in chili provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and red peppers contain iron that supports normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Spices and meat are good sources of vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from pasta
items.content: Whole‑grain macaroni adds dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Capsaicin in chili peppers has antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot chili can irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared chili sauces often contain a lot of salt; monitor the amount used.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives are needed for celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to meat and cheese; portion control is advised for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, optionally topped with grated cheese, fresh herbs, or sour cream. You can add avocado or a squeeze of lime for brightness. It is eaten with a spoon or fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stove or in a microwave, adding a splash of water to keep it moist.

content.title: About
content.content: Lentil curry with rice is a fragrant Indian-inspired dish where red or green lentils are simmered in a spiced tomato‑coconut sauce and served over fluffy rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the world’s oldest cultivated legumes, grown for over 8,000 years.
Traditional curry often uses garam masala, a blend of coriander, cumin, cardamom, and cloves.
Coconut milk softens the heat of the spices and adds a creamy texture.
The dish can be easily made vegan by using plant‑based oil instead of butter.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Lentils provide about 18 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of child‑bearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of lentils and whole‑grain rice provides a steady release of energy.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Turmeric, cumin, and coriander are rich in polyphenols that combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytates can reduce mineral absorption; soaking lentils before cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Watch sodium levels
items.content: If using pre‑made sauces, monitor salt content to avoid excess sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook lentils until partially tender, then simmer with tomato puree, coconut milk, spices, and a splash of water for 15‑20 minutes. Serve over boiled or steamed rice, garnished with fresh cilantro and lime wedges.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Freeze portions in freezer bags for up to 2 months. Reheat gently, adding a little water or broth to restore the creamy consistency.

rice-white-with-carrots-dark-green-veget.title: White Rice with Carrots, Dark Green Vegetables and Tomato‑Based Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice stir‑fried with carrots, dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach) and a tomato‑based sauce, to which a small amount of oil or butter has been added for flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple carbohydrate source for many cultures worldwide.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark green vegetables contain chlorophyll and high levels of B‑vitamins.
Tomato sauce provides lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health.
Adding a little fat helps absorb the fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice supplies quick‑acting complex carbohydrates for sustained energy.

items.title: Vitamin A from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Phytonutrients from dark green veg
items.content: Chlorophyll, folate, and vitamin K promote healthy blood and bones.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: Fat aids the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) found in the vegetables.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt, which may affect blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Fat intolerance
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to certain fats, such as butter.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Using non‑organic vegetables may leave pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or as a side to meat, fish, or legumes. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, basil) for extra aroma. You can increase the vegetable proportion or swap the added fat for olive oil if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: The salmon cake sandwich is a dish consisting of a tender salmon patty, pan‑fried to a golden crust, placed between fresh buns, often accompanied by lettuce, cucumber and a light sauce. The patty is usually made from minced salmon fillet, eggs, breadcrumbs and seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart and brain health.
The tradition of serving fish in a sandwich format began in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient fast‑food option.
Lemon juice is often added to the patty to brighten the flavor of the fish.
For extra crunch, the patty may be coated in crushed cornflakes before frying.
Fish sandwiches are frequently served with tartar sauce or a light yogurt‑based dressing.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help lower LDL cholesterol and support brain function.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Salmon provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, B6 and niacin, which aid nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides selenium, phosphorus and potassium, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, salmon is predominantly composed of healthy polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including salmon.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While salmon generally has low mercury levels, people with heightened sensitivity should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑rich due to buns, sauce and breading, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces and marinades may contain high sodium; choose low‑salt options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, cut in half. It pairs well with lettuce, fresh tomato, cucumber or avocado. For a lighter taste, use a yogurt‑herb sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked patty refrigerated for up to 2 days and store buns in a dry place. The patty can be frozen in an airtight bag for up to 3 months; reheat before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Spanish rice, no added fat is a cooked rice dish prepared in the traditional Spanish style with tomatoes, vegetables and spices, but without oil or other fats. It retains the bright flavor and aroma while keeping fat calories to a minimum.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Spanish rice (paella) is often cooked with olive oil, but the fat‑free version uses only water and vegetable broth.
Rice in Spain is mainly grown in the Valencia and Aragon regions, where the climate is ideal for high‑quality grains.
The dish is commonly served with seafood, but the fat‑free version relies solely on vegetables, making it suitable for vegetarians.
Tomatoes used in the recipe are rich in lycopene, enhancing the dish’s antioxidant profile.
The characteristic aroma is preserved by spices such as saffron, paprika and garlic, even without added fat.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat and reduced‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy release, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and saffron add lycopene and crocin, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids gut function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: While rice itself is gluten‑free, the prepared product may be made in a kitchen where gluten is present, posing a risk for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high GI, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium in broth
items.content: Flavorful vegetable broth often contains added salt, which can increase sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main dish or as a side to fish, chicken or legumes. It can be added to salads, packed in lunch boxes, or reheated in the microwave. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or cilantro for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags – they retain quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.
